blocks.text: It is the Lacerta Stellio of Hasselquist (Travels p. 351), who writes the Arabic name as Hardun. Snout very short, blunt, sloping. Jaws equal. — Nostrils in front of the eyes, at the sides of the head, near the snout, round. — Eyes at the sides of the head, in the middle. Orbit protruding at its upper margin, keeled. Brows crenate-tuberculate, pupil small, black, eyelids mobile, smooth. Crown depressed, scaly, slightly concave, raised beside the eyes. — Neck folded and wrinkled, as are the sides of the head behind the eyes. Throat with a pouch; the pouch longitudinal, compressed, keeled. Ear area hollowed out. Body depressed, ovate; sides of the abdomen protruding. Back furrowed, scaly, the scales ending in a point. Three lines of spiny tubercles on each side of the abdomen, each tubercle composed of about 7 raised, prickly scales. — Tail cylindrical, longer than the body, covered with spiny-angular scales in whorls. — Loins and legs scaly-spiny. Toes 5 on each foot, the middle ones longer. Claws curved. — Colour dusky with black and whitish spots, but it sometimes also takes on bright greenish spots and admits them on the sides of the abdomen and head, by which it comes somewhat close to the nature of the chameleon, which is thus not the only one to enjoy this faculty of changing colours. — Length of body under a span; of tail 1 span. — Habitat: ruins of Natolia, Syria and Eretz Yisrael.

Lacerta Nilotica cauda tereti longa, corpore toto glabro, squamis angulo obtuso notatis of Hasselquist, p. 361–363. "Habitat: the marshy places of Egypt near the Nile. — It is a fable of the Egyptians that this animal is generated from crocodile eggs laid on land, whereas from those laid in water come crocodiles." Hasselquist, ibid.

The Indian skink of the Arabs is without doubt the Lacerta Stincus cauda tereti mediocri, pedibus pentadactylis; digitis lobato-squamosis, squamis laevibus nitidis of Hasselquist, p. 359. "It is an error," he says on p. 361, "of almost all authors that they have believed the sea skink to be a fish."
Whoever wants more should consult ABDOLLATIF, Compendium Memorabilium Aegypti, book 1, Chapter 3, p. 42 ff.
It only swells up when it is provoked, according to Hasselquist, who carefully observed this animal himself and describes it accurately in his Travels p. 348–351, German trans.
